name: Kwomtari
confidence_why: The only phonological description, Drew 2008 (Baifeni dialect, frame elicitation), states that stress is neither contrastive nor consistent, and the sole dissent, a preliminary SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (2004, from Honsberger and Honsberger 1997) listing three apparent stress pairs, warns in the same document that stress will not be written until further analysis and that the researchers' hearing was uncertain, while its own authors later edited the 2008 volume and let Drew's conclusion stand.

catalog_quote: The Kwomtari language does not exhibit contrasts in nasalisation, tone or vowel length. The only suprasegmental worthy of discussion in this section is stress. Stress is difficult to hear; often syllables seem to carry equal stress, or a given word is pronounced with different stress on different occasions. There are no examples of contrastive stress. In a bisyllabic word uttered in isolation, the first syllable often sounds stronger, but the second syllable carries rising pitch. As noted in §2.2, a syllable containing schwa is not stressed (with the single exception of /mənə/ [ˈmənə]), so a word containing schwa in its initial syllable will normally have its stress on the second syllable. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: No contrastive stress, no tone or length contrast. Stress is hard to hear and inconsistent across repetitions. Bisyllables in isolation: first syllable often stronger, but the second carries rising pitch. In carrier frames every word, affixed or not, was stressed on the final syllable. A schwa syllable is never stressed when other vowels are present (sole exception /'mənə/ 'I'), so schwa-initial words stress the second syllable (p. 29: 'Schwa never receives stress when other vowels are present in a word. The sole instance of a stressed schwa is the word /mənə/ [mənə], in which the initial schwa is stressed.'). Drew closes: 'The analysis of stress remains uncertain, but since stress does not seem to operate contrastively (or even consistently), this subject may be regarded as worthy of further study but not significant in Kwomtari phonology.' (p. 43)
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 43: 'Words of more than two syllables also exhibited secondary stress, which fell on the first syllable of three and four syllable words, and the second syllable of five syllable words. The two stresses (second syllable and final syllable) in five syllable words often sounded equal.' (frame condition)
new_statements.exceptions: Schwa never stressed when other vowels are present; single exception /mənə/ [ˈmənə] 'I' (pp. 29, 42). Isolation vs. frame placement differs (initial-strong vs. final). The earlier SIL-PNG Organised Phonology Data sheet (2004, held as, p. 4) claims 'There is evidence of contrast in stress: 'mune 'I,me' / mu'naglu 'heart', 'ite 'house' / ì'te 'here', 'yeri 'lime powder' / ye'ré 'west'' and (p. 5) 'Stress will not be written until futher analysis on it is completed.'; Drew 2008 supersedes this with the explicit statement that there are no examples of contrastive stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Drew 2008 p. 17: 'This paper is based on data collected from the Baifeni dialect' (data collected by the Honsbergers 1990-97 plus Drew's 1998 stay at Baifeni). The introduction (pp. 1-15) names six Kwomtari-speaking villages (Baifeni, Kwomtari, Yanebi, Wagreni, Yaur, and one more on the three rivers) with Baifeni 'the most central village geographically and linguistically' (p. 3).

readall_conflicts: Within the one descriptive source there is an internal tension that Drew herself flags: isolation bisyllables sound initial-strong (with rising pitch on the second syllable) while carrier-frame elicitation gives uniform final stress, so she concludes stress is neither contrastive nor consistent. The only outside disagreement is the earlier SIL-PNG Organised Phonology Data sheet (2004), which lists minimal-looking pairs ('mune vs mu'naglu, 'ite vs i'te, 'yeri vs ye're) as 'evidence of contrast in stress'; Drew 2008 (same SIL programme, fuller data, frame elicitation) states there are no examples of contrastive stress, and her schwa rule (/mənə/ the sole stressed schwa; schwa-initial words stress syllable 2) plus isolation/frame variation account for those pairs. Baron 1983 (survey, downloaded 2026-09-16) is silent on Kwomtari stress. No other source exists per Glottolog (all three descriptive refs are this 2008 volume).

audit.reasoning: (1) Deciding quotation confirmed verbatim in the Drew 2008 text we hold at the stated locators (section 5 pp. 42-43; section 2.2 p. 29), and the OPD 2004 contra-quote also confirmed verbatim. (2) The classification rests on the only phonological description of the language, a 2008 SIL phonology sketch with an explicit suprasegmentals section and frame elicitation; Glottolog's full descriptive bibliography is this single volume, and web search found nothing newer or instrumental (only Baron 1983 survey, downloaded, silent). (3) No unheld work would improve the record; list of works to obtain empty. (4) Coding 'variable' (no contrastive stress, inconsistent placement, phrase-final prominence in frames, schwa unstressable) faithfully reflects Drew's own hedged conclusion; the earlier OPD 'lexical' reading is superseded by the later, fuller analysis from the same SIL programme. Status well-sourced; no action.
